Erwin Schrödinger was an Austrian-Irish theoretical physicist who developed wave mechanics, a revolutionary formulation of quantum mechanics based on wave motion rather than particles. He formulated the fundamental equation governing how the quantum wavefunction changes over time, and he proposed the famous thought experiment known as Schrödinger's cat. In 1933, he shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac.

In 1925, Schrödinger formulated his now-legendary equation, a partial differential equation that describes how the wavefunction — represented by the Greek letter psi — of a quantum system evolves through time. This equation became the cornerstone of quantum mechanics, providing a way to calculate the probability of finding a particle at any given location.

Ten years later, in 1935, Schrödinger proposed the thought experiment we now call Schrödinger's cat to illustrate the profound problems with quantum superposition. Imagine a sealed box containing a cat, a radioactive atom, a Geiger counter, and a flask of poison. If the atom decays, the counter triggers and releases the poison, killing the cat. If it doesn't decay, the cat lives. According to quantum mechanics, until someone opens the box and observes the outcome, the atom exists in a superposition of both decayed and non-decayed states — which means the cat is simultaneously both alive and dead. This thought experiment highlights the absurdity of applying quantum rules to everyday objects.

Schrödinger proved the mathematical equivalence of his wave mechanics and Werner Heisenberg's matrix mechanics, despite the two theories using completely different mathematical formalisms. He had developed wave mechanics partly because he found Heisenberg's matrix mechanics too abstract and difficult to visualize. He also coined the term quantum entanglement — Verschränkung in German — to describe the correlated states of separated particles, an idea he developed while analyzing Einstein's EPR paradox.

In 1944, Schrödinger wrote the influential book "What Is Life?" which explored genetics from a physicist's perspective. This book inspired James Watson and Francis Crick to study the structure of DNA. Albert Einstein praised Schrödinger's wave mechanics and collaborated with him on criticisms of the Copenhagen interpretation, including the cat thought experiment itself. Niels Bohr hosted Schrödinger in Copenhagen to debate wave mechanics, and eventually incorporated his wave equation into the Copenhagen interpretation framework.
